content: If mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is used to diagnose severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in a child, it should also be used to monitor and confirm nutritional recovery. Similarly, if weight-for-height is the diagnostic criterion for SAM, it should be used for assessing and confirming recovery. Children admitted with bilateral pitting edema alone should be discharged based on the anthropometric indicator (MUAC or weight-for-height) routinely used in the program. Percentage weight gain should not be used as a discharge criterion. This is a strong recommendation, though based on low-quality evidence. Necessary resources and services must be in place if children are referred to outpatient care. Danger signs requiring immediate attention include inability to drink or breastfeed, persistent vomiting, history of convulsions (more than one or lasting over 15 minutes), lethargy or unconsciousness, and ongoing convulsions. Children with SAM and severe bilateral edema (+++) should be admitted for inpatient care, even if they have no medical complications and have an appetite. This is a strong recommendation, though based on very low-quality evidence. Children with uncomplicated SAM who do not require inpatient care and are managed as outpatients should receive a course of oral antibiotics, such as amoxicillin. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Children who are undernourished but do not have SAM should not routinely receive antibiotics unless there are clinical signs of infection. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Children with SAM should receive the daily recommended nutrient intake of vitamin A throughout the treatment period. This can be provided as part of therapeutic foods or a multi-micronutrient formulation. A daily dose of approximately 5000 IU of vitamin A is recommended. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Children with SAM do not require high-dose vitamin A supplementation if they are receiving F-75, F-100, or ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) that complies with WHO specifications, as these already contain sufficient vitamin A. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Children with SAM should receive a high dose of vitamin A (50,000 IU, 100,000 IU, or 200,000 IU depending on age) upon admission only if the therapeutic foods they are given are not fortified as per WHO specifications and vitamin A is not part of other daily supplements. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Children with SAM and acute or persistent diarrhea can be given RUTF in the same way as children without diarrhea, whether managed as inpatients or outpatients. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. In inpatient settings, once children with SAM are stabilized, have an appetite, and reduced edema, they should transition from F-75 to RUTF over 2–3 days, as tolerated. The recommended energy intake during this period is 100–135 kcal/kg/day. The optimal approach for achieving this may depend on the number and skills of staff available to supervise feeding and monitor the children during rehabilitation. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Two options for transitioning children from F-75 to RUTF are suggested: 1. Begin feeding with RUTF as prescribed for the transition phase, allowing the child to drink water freely. If the child does not consume the prescribed amount of RUTF, supplement with F-75. Gradually increase the amount of RUTF over 2–3 days until the child meets the full requirement. 2. Provide the prescribed amount of RUTF for the transition phase, allowing the child to drink water freely. If the child consumes less than half the prescribed amount of RUTF in the first 12 hours, stop RUTF and revert to F-75. Retry the same approach after 1–2 days until the child consumes the appropriate amount of RUTF to meet energy needs. Children with SAM who are HIV-infected and qualify for lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) should start ART as soon as possible after stabilization of metabolic complications and sepsis. Stabilization is indicated by the return of appetite and resolution of severe edema. HIV-infected children with SAM should receive the same ART regimens and doses as HIV-infected children without SAM. Close monitoring is required during the first 6–8 weeks of ART initiation to identify early metabolic complications and opportunistic infections. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. HIV-infected children with SAM should be managed with the same therapeutic feeding approaches as children with SAM who are not HIV-infected. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. HIV-infected children with SAM should receive a high dose of vitamin A upon admission (50,000 IU to 200,000 IU depending on age) and zinc for diarrhea management, unless they are already receiving F-75, F-100, or RUTF fortified according to WHO specifications. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Infants under 6 months of age with SAM and complicating factors (e.g., serious clinical conditions, recent weight loss, ineffective feeding, or pitting edema) should be admitted for inpatient care. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Feeding approaches for infants under 6 months with SAM should prioritize establishing or re-establishing effective exclusive breastfeeding by the mother or caregiver. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Infants under 6 months with SAM who are admitted should be breastfed where possible, and mothers or caregivers should be supported to breastfeed. If breastfeeding is not possible, support should be provided to re-lactate or encourage wet nursing. Supplementary feeding may include expressed breast milk, commercial infant formula, or F-75, depending on the infant's condition. Undiluted F-100 should not be given due to the risk of hypernatremic dehydration. Infants under 6 months with SAM can be transferred to outpatient care when all clinical conditions or complications are resolved, they have a good appetite, are clinically well and alert, and have adequate weight gain. They should also have been checked for immunizations and linked to community-based follow-up and support. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. Infants under 6 months can be discharged from all care when they are breastfeeding effectively or feeding well with replacement feeds, have adequate weight gain, and achieve a weight-for-length ≥ –2 Z-score. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence.
